editorNote: Behind closed doors, a multimedia machine called Lorraine hints at a startling future while software giants battle to put every office task under one roof.
morningLine: Amiga shows its colors, Symphony meets Framework, and Marvel's Hulk crashes into the adventure-game aisle.

lead.headline: Behind Closed Doors, Amiga's Lorraine Points to a New Generation
lead.dek: A rough but dazzling 68000 prototype promises color, sound, animation, speech, and communications in one home machine.
body: Visitors invited behind closed doors at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show saw something very different from another beige box. Amiga's Lorraine prototype, now detailed in COMPUTE!'s August issue, paired a Motorola 68000 processor with custom graphics and sound hardware intended to make animation, music, and multitasking central parts of personal computing.

The proposed machine carried 128K of memory expandable to 512K internally, 64K of ROM, a built-in 320K double-sided floppy drive, and a 300-bps modem that could be replaced by a 1200-bps unit. Its video design promised 320-by-200 and 640-by-200 modes, a palette of 4,096 colors, eight independent sprites, split screens, and frame-buffer animation, while four audio channels and text-to-speech voices rounded out the demonstration.

Those specifications put Lorraine in territory normally reserved for expensive workstations and specialized video gear. COMPUTE! writer Selby Bateman judged the potential machine powerful enough to make an IBM PC look like a four-function calculator, a startling comparison at a show otherwise dominated by software and cautious refinements to familiar hardware.

Yet the demonstration remained a promise, not a product. The rough prototype was operated from a remote terminal, Amiga still needed substantial capital and production engineering, and its claimed $1,500 price and Christmas delivery faced a severe test. Even with those cautions, Lorraine offered the clearest glimpse this summer of a home computer designed from the start for sight, sound, and motion.

stories.headline: Symphony and Framework Fight to Define Integrated Software
body: The business-software aisle has become a contest over the shape of the electronic office. Lotus Symphony combines spreadsheet, word processing, database, communications, and graphics functions in a $695 package, extending the formula that made Lotus 1-2-3 the defining program of the IBM PC.

Ashton-Tate's Framework approaches the same goal through outlining and nested frames able to contain text, spreadsheets, graphs, and other documents. Developed by Robert Carr's Forefront and marketed with Ashton-Tate's muscle, it asks users to organize work as connected pieces rather than separate application files.

PC Magazine, dated August 7, calls the two products pace-setters and recalls Lotus and Ashton-Tate occupying adjacent Spring COMDEX booths like technological knights preparing for battle. Their rivalry makes one point clear: the next office-software prize may belong to the package that keeps users from leaving it.

stories.headline: Compaq Deskpro Turns Compatibility into a Speed Contest
body: Compaq is arguing that IBM compatibility need not mean IBM performance. Its Deskpro runs an 8086 at 7.14 MHz, delivering a reported two to three times the speed of the PC while retaining a slowdown mode for programs whose timing depends on IBM's pace.

Four models stretch from a 128K single-floppy system at $2,495 to a 640K flagship with a 10MB hard disk and 10MB cartridge-tape backup at $7,195. Eight expansion slots, an 8087 socket, and extensive card and software testing make the machine a direct bid for serious PC buyers.

The mini-data-cartridge tape unit shares the floppy controller to trim parts and cost. Peter Norton called the new machine what the PC-XT should have been; whether buyers agree, the Deskpro has turned compatibility into a race to improve on the standard rather than merely copy it.

stories.headline: Questprobe Sends the Hulk into the Adventure Machine
body: Adventure International and Marvel are joining comics and computer adventures in Questprobe featuring The Hulk, announced for August on the Commodore 64 and Plus/4. The green giant leads a planned line that treats familiar comic heroes as interactive characters rather than static licensed decoration.

The announcement lands amid a strong software summer. Spinnaker's Trillium label is adapting science-fiction novels including Rendezvous with Rama, Fahrenheit 451, and Starman Jones, with Michael Crichton scripting Amazon and Arthur C. Clarke devising an ending for Rama.

COMPUTE! also supplies games readers can type themselves: Devastator and Jackpot appear across VIC-20, Commodore 64, Atari, IBM PC/PCjr, and Apple editions. From superhero licenses to literary adaptations and printed listings, the game shelf is widening in every direction.

stories.headline: IBM's Price Cuts Put PC-Compatible Makers in a Squeeze
body: IBM's June price reductions are still rippling across the August market. A 256K PC with one 360K drive now lists at $1,995, the two-drive version at $2,420, and the 128K XT system unit has fallen from $4,995 to $4,275.

The enhanced 128K PCjr with a disk drive dropped from $1,269 to $999. Those reductions, roughly 18 to 23 percent across key computer prices, force compatible makers to answer an opponent with far greater scale and an instantly recognized badge.

Eagle Computer matched the cuts while negotiating with creditors over $10.8 million in unsecured loans after a disastrous quarter. As analyst Esther Dyson warned, firms that play with price invite IBM to come at them with price.

bbsNote.headline: Modems Move from Add-On to Built-In Feature
bbsNote.summary: Lorraine, AdamLink, and Videotex 64 all treat telecommunications as an increasingly central part of the home-computer experience.

posts.text: A replaceable 300-bps modem design suggests that going online could become a standard system feature.
Coleco pairs a direct-connect 300-baud full-duplex modem with AdamLink software.
Videotex 64 promises to mix color pictures with text and transmit them over normal phone lines.

curiosity.headline: A Preschool Keyboard Built Like a Tiny School Desk
curiosity.summary: Koala's $79.95 Muppet Learning Keys replaces conventional keys with a child's desk full of learning objects.
curiosity.detail: The three-pound Apple II/Commodore 64 accessory includes a ruler, watercolor set, penmanship slate, compass, eraser, and arithmetic book, with Kermit, Miss Piggy, and Gonzo guiding alphabet, number, color, and shape exercises.
